passage:
Ujjwal: Pitch done. I want to disappear.
Reena: 😬 The chart?
Ujjwal: Revenue doubling every quarter for three years. Mrs Kapoor asked where the doubling comes from. I said "momentum".
Reena: And she said?
Ujjwal: How many new clinics per quarter, and how many people to close them? I had no numbers. She wasn't angry, just tired. Like she'd seen this slide too many times.
Reena: Ouch.
Ujjwal: Then she started doubting other slides too, even the cost page, and that one was solid.
Reena: Next time we build the line from real monthly sign-ups and show the range.
Ujjwal: Yes. Sorry, I made us look careless.

qa.q: How long did the chart show revenue doubling every quarter?
qa.a: The chart showed it for three years.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling after the pitch?
qa.a: Ujjwal was embarrassed and deflated, as the wish to disappear and the apology for making them look careless show.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do differently with the next revenue chart?
qa.a: Ujjwal could build the line from real monthly sign-ups and show a range, so each assumption can be traced and defended.

qa.q: How might Mrs Kapoor have seen the chart?
qa.a: Mrs Kapoor probably saw a familiar, unsupported slide, and since one weak claim made her doubt the rest, the whole deck lost some trust. 🤔

grounding: The chat shows a founder presenting a doubling-revenue chart with no basis, which an investor quickly questions, lowering trust in the whole deck.

passage:
At the agri-startup fair in the district hall, fans creaking overhead, Deepak had eight minutes on stage for his banana-ripening chambers. His last slide was the one he was proudest of: revenue doubling every quarter for three years, ending in a tall green bar.
In the question round, Zubin, who had backed three cold-storage companies, raised a hand. "Doubling every quarter. Based on what? How many chambers are running now?"
"Four."
"And how many farmers have paid twice?"
"Two... but the demand is huge."
"Then why double and not triple? Or halve?" Zubin asked, not unkindly. "If this slide is a guess, I have to wonder which of the others are too."
The hall went quiet. Deepak's ears burned. After the session, two investors who had been nodding earlier left without taking his card.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when his ears burned?
qa.a: Deepak felt embarrassed and exposed, realising the chart he was proudest of had cost him credibility.

qa.q: What could Deepak have shown instead of the doubling chart?
qa.a: The real numbers from the four chambers and repeat farmers, with a modest forecast and the reasons behind it.

qa.q: How does Zubin see the rest of the deck after that chart?
qa.a: Zubin begins to doubt the other slides too, wondering which of them are also guesses.

grounding: It shows a founder presenting revenue doubling every quarter with no basis, an experienced investor questioning it in minutes, and the whole pitch losing credibility.

passage:
In a glass meeting room in Toronto, Dalia clicked to slide nine: a steep chart for her tutoring marketplace, revenue doubling every quarter until it touched ten million in year three. She had made it the night before, after seeing a similar slide in a famous startup's deck.
Kaito, a partner who had funded education companies for fifteen years, leaned in. "Walk me through quarter two. Where do the new tutors come from?"
"Word of mouth, mostly."
"And your current growth?"
"Twelve percent last quarter."
"So from twelve percent to a hundred. What changes?" He waited. Dalia started to explain, then stopped.
Kaito closed the laptop gently. "I like the problem you're solving. But now I'm not sure how to read any of your numbers." The meeting ended fifteen minutes early.

qa.q: What was Dalia's growth last quarter?
What was Dalia feeling when she started to explain, then stopped?
qa.a: Dalia felt flustered and exposed, realising she had no basis for the doubling chart.

qa.q: What would you change first in Dalia's deck?
qa.a: Replace the steep chart with the real twelve percent growth and a forecast whose reasons she can explain.

qa.q: How does Kaito see Dalia's numbers after slide nine?
qa.a: Kaito likes the problem but no longer trusts any of the numbers, so the meeting ends early.

grounding: It shows a founder's unfounded chart of revenue doubling each quarter being questioned by a seasoned investor within minutes, undermining the whole pitch.
